clue.text: Assistant to D. G. Rossetti and naval officer's friend

definitions.meaning: at the close of John Fowles's novel the heroine is found working as an amanuensis in the Chelsea house of the painter-poet
the 'French Lieutenant' of Fowles's title is a naval officer, Varguennes, whose supposed lover she is

explanation.surface: A list of credentials for a Victorian woman who knew a painter and a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves describe the heroine of John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman: gossip makes her the lover of a French naval lieutenant, and she ends the book in Rossetti's household.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowles's heroine is both the woman linked to the French naval lieutenant and, by the end, a helper in the Rossetti home.

clue.text: Mendelssohn's blended whisky?

parts.note: names a Mendelssohn work while pretending to describe a harmonious mixture of the spirit distilled north of the border

explanation.definitionFit: Mendelssohn's Third is known by a nickname naming Scotland, and a blend of that country's whisky could also be called a harmonious mix of it.

clue.text: Burnt ones leave ash on an old man's sleeve, wrote T. S. Eliot

definitions.text: Burnt ones leave ash on an old man's sleeve, wrote T. S. Eliot

parts.words: Burnt ones leave ash on an old man's sleeve, wrote T. S. Eliot
parts.note: recalls lines in Little Gidding: 'Ash on an old man's sleeve / Is all the ash the burnt ... leave', the flowers left unnamed

explanation.surface: A line of Eliot about what burnt things leave behind on an old man's sleeve.
explanation.definitionFit: In Eliot's Little Gidding the burnt flowers whose ash settles on an old man's sleeve are the garden blooms of the English rose bed.

clue.text: Chic Moore I rewrite, showing high burlesque style

indicators.note: to rewrite these words is to set their letters down again in a new order

explanation.surface: A reviewer asks to redo a piece on someone called Chic Moore, which turns out lofty and comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' rearranges the ten letters of CHIC MOORE I. The definition is a literary term for mock-epic writing that treats a trivial subject in a lofty manner.
explanation.definitionFit: High burlesque is the mock-heroic mode, mixing epic grandeur with comedy, which is just what the compound adjective describes.

clue.text: Where to find followers of St Philip Neri showing rhetorical skill

definitions.text: Where to find followers of St Philip Neri
definitions.meaning: St Philip Neri founded a congregation of priests whose houses, like the London one at Brompton, take this name
the art of public speaking, eloquence

explanation.surface: Praise for the eloquence of a saint's disciples.
explanation.definitionFit: Neri's congregation is named for its prayer-hall, and the same word means the art of eloquent public speaking.

clue.text: Motown associated by Runyon with David's prophet

definitions.meaning: the nickname of the Michigan car city, from 'motor town'

definitions.text: associated by Runyon with David's prophet
definitions.meaning: Nathan was the prophet who rebuked King David; Damon Runyon's gambler Nathan carries the city's name as his surname

explanation.surface: A city that Damon Runyon somehow ties to a biblical prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: Nathan, the prophet in King David's story, shares his first name with Runyon's crap-game organiser, whose surname is the Michigan city (the character of Guys and Dolls).
explanation.definitionFit: Motown is the nickname of the Michigan motor city, and Runyon's gambler Nathan bears that city as his surname.

clue.text: Mr Geller's blockbuster writer

definitions.meaning: Uri Geller is the spoon-bending entertainer, so 'Mr Geller's' is his first name with an apostrophe-s
Leon, author of the bestseller Exodus

explanation.surface: The best-selling author associated with the spoon-bending Mr Geller.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Mr Geller's' as Uri's and run it together: that gives the surname of Leon, the American author of Exodus.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the spoon-bender plus a possessive spells the surname of the novelist of Exodus and other bestsellers.

clue.text: "When 'Dulce est desipere in loco' / Was written, real — winged the pen" (Calverley)

definitions.text: "When 'Dulce est desipere in loco' / Was written, real — winged the pen" (Calverley)

parts.words: "When 'Dulce est desipere in loco' / Was written, real — winged the pen" (Calverley)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from C. S. Calverley's verse: the missing word names the Roman wine that inspired Horace's line

explanation.surface: A gap in Calverley's lines about the wine that fuelled Horace when he wrote 'it is sweet to be foolish at times'.
explanation.definitionFit: Calverley says genuine wine from the Roman Campanian vineyards spurred Horace's pen; that famous classical vintage fills the blank.

clue.text: The future Mrs Trundle is a beauty in Italy, a minor to the French

parts.note: taken as written
bella is Italian for a beautiful woman
a ward is a minor under a guardian's care
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A future bride from Dickens is described as an Italian beauty, still underage, travelling to France.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Pickwick Papers Mr Trundle marries the daughter of old Mr Wardle of Dingley Dell; 'to' only links the last piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In Pickwick Papers the Dingley Dell daughter becomes the bride of Mr Trundle, so she is the Mrs Trundle to be.

clue.text: Honour to Robin Maugham character for paying close attention

annotationWithheld.why: Honour to Robin Maugham character for paying close attention (9): SERVANT is Robin Maugham's The Servant, but 'Honour' would have to give OB, which is no recognised honour (OBE has a third letter E); the parse needs a word the clue as held lacks
annotationWithheld.clue: Honour to Robin Maugham character for paying close attention

clue.text: Ulysses felt that they might touch the Happy ones, Tennyson tells us

definitions.text: Ulysses felt that they might touch the Happy ones, Tennyson tells us

parts.words: Ulysses felt that they might touch the Happy ones, Tennyson tells us
parts.note: recalls Tennyson's Ulysses: 'It may be we shall touch the Happy ...', the blessed lands of the west

explanation.surface: Tennyson's aged hero hopes to reach the happy places across the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tennyson's poem Ulysses hopes his crew may reach the Happy ___, the Islands of the Blessed in the western ocean.

clue.text: Gloves with heavy weights for heavyweights in Rome

definitions.text: Gloves with heavy weights for heavyweights in Rome

parts.words: Gloves with heavy weights for heavyweights in Rome
parts.note: describes the leather thongs loaded with lead or iron that Roman boxers bound round their fists

explanation.surface: Weighted boxing gloves worn by the big fighters of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavyweights' plays on boxing's weight division; the Latin plural of cestus names the Roman fighters' weighted hand-wraps.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural names the leather hand-straps, weighted with metal, that Roman pugilists wore in the ring.

clue.text: Order rings from Melville

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
two Os, each letter shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A command that some rings be taken from a man called Melville.
explanation.definitionFit: Melville's 1847 South Seas novel, sequel to Typee, carries this Polynesian title, so it is a book from Melville.

clue.text: Street of hungry authors?

parts.note: the old London street that gave its name to impoverished hack writers, read as a street named for food

explanation.surface: Where starving writers live.
explanation.walkthrough: The old London street lent its name to penniless hack writers; its first word is also slang for food, which hungry authors lack.
explanation.definitionFit: The London street became a byword for poor hacks, and its name is also slang for food, which such hungry writers crave.

clue.text: Drudge who finally got out (first ball)

definitions.text: Drudge who finally got out (first ball)

parts.words: Drudge who finally got out (first ball)
parts.note: the kitchen drudge of the fairy tale who at last escaped to the prince's ball; 'out first ball' sounds like cricket

explanation.surface: A cricketer dismissed on the first delivery, after a long wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out (first ball)' suggests a batsman dismissed by the first delivery in cricket, but the drudge is the fairy-tale heroine who got out of the house to her first ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale kitchen drudge finally escaped her chores to attend the royal dance, and her name means any overlooked menial.

clue.text: Descriptive of one of Falstaff's recruits

definitions.text: Descriptive of one of Falstaff's recruits

parts.words: Descriptive of one of Falstaff's recruits
parts.note: in Henry IV Part 2 Falstaff's recruits are Mouldy, Wart, Feeble, Bullcalf and a thin man named for a dark silhouette; the adjective from his name is wanted

explanation.surface: An adjective fitting one of the ragged soldiers Falstaff enlists.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff's recruits in Henry IV Part 2 have descriptive names; add -Y to the thin one's name to make the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff's thin recruit is named for a dark outline cast by light, and the adjective from that name means dim or indistinct.

clue.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

definitions.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

parts.words: From which Rex Warner's career took off?
parts.note: Rex Warner's best-known novel (1941) is named for an airfield, the place planes take off from

explanation.surface: Asking where a novelist's career got off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Rex Warner's 1941 novel is titled after an airfield, so 'took off' works both for the career and for aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: Warner's best-known novel bears the old word for an airfield, the place from which aircraft take off.

clue.text: "The sight of — personalities decomposing in the eternity of print" (Virginia Woolf)

definitions.text: "The sight of — personalities decomposing in the eternity of print" (Virginia Woolf)

parts.words: "The sight of — personalities decomposing in the eternity of print" (Virginia Woolf)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Virginia Woolf: the missing adjective describes petty personalities

explanation.surface: Woolf deplores the sight of petty people rotting forever in print.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's missing adjective means petty or of little importance, describing the personalities she sees preserved in print.

clue.text: Scott character, author of The Antiquary

definitions.text: Scott character, author of The Antiquary

parts.words: Scott character, author of The Antiquary
parts.note: the knight who is hero of Scott's verse romance of Flodden; Scott is also the author of The Antiquary

explanation.surface: A character who is also said to have written a Scott novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma reads as if the character wrote The Antiquary; in fact both phrases point to Walter Scott, who wrote The Antiquary and the verse tale of Flodden named for its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord ___ is the title knight of Scott's 1808 poem about Flodden Field, by the author who also wrote The Antiquary.

clue.text: Heroine's assistant is snare, perhaps, in court

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of these words might be laid out another way

explanation.surface: A heroine's helper is set up as a trap during a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the rearrangement. Portia's waiting-woman in The Merchant of Venice follows her into the trial scene disguised as a lawyer's clerk, which is why the clue says 'in court'.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice Portia's lady-in-waiting serves the heroine and attends her, disguised as a clerk, at the trial.

clue.text: Hindu school of philosophy braved antagonism, to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A school of Indian thought bravely faced hostility, up to a point.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upanishad-based system is one of the six orthodox schools of Indian thought.

clue.text: Viking coast — French wine area?

parts.note: vin is the French word for wine
land is a region or tract of ground

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Norse shoreline is a French wine-growing district.
explanation.walkthrough: Leif Erikson's Norsemen named the North American shore they found for its grapes, which the French-wine reading echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse sagas give this name to the North American shore Leif Erikson reached around AD 1000.

clue.text: Irish poet in London park

definitions.meaning: Douglas, Gaelic scholar, poet and first President of Ireland
the large royal park by Marble Arch whose first word is this name

explanation.surface: An Irish poet strolling in a London park.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas ___ was a poet and Ireland's first President; the same surname begins the name of London's big park by Marble Arch.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas, the Gaelic poet who became Ireland's first President, shares his surname with the big royal park in central London.

clue.text: Architect reveals some low rent accommodation

indicators.note: some says only a part of the following words is wanted, a run inside them

explanation.surface: A designer exposes some cheap housing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes a run from 'low rent': the last letter of one word and the first three of the next. Sir Christopher is the architect of St Paul's.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher designed St Paul's Cathedral and many City of London churches.

clue.text: Regretted a Spanish dramatist ()

parts.note: to regret something is to have rued it

explanation.surface: A Spanish playwright who had second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: Lope de ___ was a sixteenth-century actor-playwright of Seville, an early figure of the Spanish stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lope de ___ was an early Spanish playwright and actor-manager of the 1500s.

clue.text: Small bag, and in Paris, very small

parts.note: et is French for 'and'
wee is Scottish for tiny

explanation.surface: A tiny French handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: This is an old English spelling of etui, a small case for needles or cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui (spelt here the old English way) is a small ornamental case for needles or toiletries.

clue.text: An extension in name only for the author of His House in Order

definitions.meaning: a part added to a building

definitions.text: in name only for the author of His House in Order
definitions.meaning: the playwright Arthur ___ Pinero wrote that play, and this is his middle name only

explanation.surface: Asking whether a playwright's house was extended only in name.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur ___ Pinero wrote the 1906 comedy His House in Order; this word is only his middle name, so it is 'in name only' for him.
explanation.definitionFit: A side annex of a building has this name, and so does the middle of Pinero's three names.

clue.text: I am no substitute for Miss Mitchison

indicators.note: to substitute is to put other forms in place, so these letters stand in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to stand in for a woman called Mitchison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'substitute' rearranges I AM NO into the first name of the Scottish novelist Mitchison.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish writer Mitchison, author of The Corn King and the Spring Queen, had this given name.

clue.text: "Being bitten in half by a shark is a compromise by with being whole" (P. J. O'Rourke)

definitions.text: "Being bitten in half by a shark is a compromise by with being whole" (P. J. O'Rourke)

parts.words: "Being bitten in half by a shark is a compromise by with being whole" (P. J. O'Rourke)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the American humorist O'Rourke, where 'compromise by' is printed in place of the missing participle

explanation.surface: A humorist's quip that being bitten in two by a shark is a compromise.
explanation.walkthrough: O'Rourke's line is that being bitten in half is a compromise between being left alone and being eaten in one piece; the printed clue garbles the gap, but the missing word means gulped down.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means gulped down entire, the alternative to being bitten in two.

clue.text: Man-made legend distorted by Graham Greene

indicators.note: distorted means twisted out of shape, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man-made legend is twisted by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distorted' rearranges MAN-MADE LEGEND into the title of Greene's 1935 novel set in Stockholm.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's 1935 novel about an Englishman working in Stockholm has this title, so it is a work by him.
